problem: PEFT gains on SAM are attributed to pretrained knowledge, but no control isolates the pretraining contribution from the generic benefit of optimizing a head/adapters over any high-dimensional feature bank.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On simple adaptation domains (high-contrast, texture-separable), LoRA + decoder training over a frozen randomly-initialized encoder reaches a nontrivial fraction of pretrained-SAM adaptation performance, and the pretraining premium (pretrained minus random) varies enormously across benchmarks - exposing which benchmarks actually test foundation knowledge.
falsifiable_prediction: The pretraining premium measured across 8 benchmarks will span a wide range (from small to dominant); benchmarks with small premiums will be those where the frozen-feature null (W15-B001-A-073) is also strong - convergent evidence they don't measure adaptation of knowledge.
why_important: Establishes the missing control condition for the entire adaptation literature; premium-scoring benchmarks tells the field where foundation-model claims are actually being tested - a calibration exercise with broad reuse.
why_possibly_novel: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] Random-feature baselines exist in representation-learning literature; [HYPOTHESIS] using them to price the pretraining premium in SAM PEFT benchmarks appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 8 benchmarks x {pretrained, random-frozen} encoders x identical LoRA/decoder recipe x 2 seeds; report premium distribution; correlate with null-baseline strength.
main_risk: Random encoders may need different optimization settings for fairness; use LR sweeps for both arms.
community_default_belief: Adaptation performance flows from pretrained representations; a random encoder would be near-useless, so the control is skipped as obviously unnecessary.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Random projections preserve substantial information (classic random-features results); with a trainable decoder and adapters, 'obviously useless' has repeatedly proven wrong in ML history - and the premium has never been measured here.
fastest_falsification: Six hours: one easy + one hard benchmark with random encoder; near-zero performance on both falsifies the interesting version.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: The foundation-model tax: on narrow, high-volume domains, a small from-scratch specialist beats LoRA-adapted SAM at matched TOTAL cost (labels + compute + inference).
problem: Adapting SAM is the default for new segmentation tasks; the regime where this default loses to small specialists on full-cost accounting is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For domains that are narrow (low appearance diversity) and inference-heavy (deployment cost dominates), the total-cost frontier favors compact specialists once labeled data exceeds a threshold; the threshold is predictable from domain diversity measures - giving a decision rule for when NOT to use foundation models.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 6 domains spanning diversity levels, the specialist-vs-adapted-SAM crossover (in labels) will exist for low-diversity domains and correlate with measured feature-space diversity; for high-diversity domains no crossover will appear within practical budgets.
why_important: Anti-hype calibration with an actionable rule: the field lacks quantified guidance on when foundation adaptation is the wrong tool; inference-cost asymmetry (ViT-H vs tiny UNet-class models [KNOWN FACT] orders of magnitude apart in FLOPs) makes this economically significant at scale.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] A predictive crossover rule based on domain-diversity measurement, under total-cost accounting, appears absent; existing comparisons fix budgets arbitrarily.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 6 domains: train specialist (compact segmentation net) and LoRA-SAM at label budgets {50..5000}; measure accuracy and full costs; locate crossovers; regress on diversity metrics.
main_risk: Specialist architecture choice is a degree of freedom critics will attack; fix one standard compact architecture a priori.
community_default_belief: Foundation-model adaptation dominates from-scratch training in the low-and-medium data regime, and label efficiency justifies inference cost.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Narrow domains cap the value of general priors while the priors' inference cost is paid on every prediction forever; the accounting favors specialists earlier than the label-efficiency narrative suggests.
fastest_falsification: One day: one narrow domain (e.g., fixed-camera industrial) at 2 budgets; no crossover trend falsifies for that regime.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Averaging beats capacity: souping LoRAs from different seeds on the SAME task outperforms doubling rank - PEFT is variance-limited, not capacity-limited.
problem: When adaptation underperforms, the reflex is more capacity (rank); the alternative diagnosis - solution variance from the init lottery (W15-B001-A-013) - implies a different, cheaper fix.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In common SAM adaptation regimes, weight-averaging k rank-r LoRAs (same data, different seeds) improves test IoU more than training one rank-kr LoRA at equal total compute, because the binding constraint is estimation variance, not expressivity.
falsifiable_prediction: Soup-of-4-rank-8 will beat rank-32 across most tested domains at matched compute; the soup advantage will shrink as training data grows (variance shrinks) and vanish on tasks where measured intrinsic rank exceeds 8 (capacity binds) - a two-regime prediction tying to W15-B001-A-012.
why_important: Practical (free accuracy at deployment via averaging) and diagnostic: locates where adaptation sits on the bias-variance frontier, informing whether future method work should target capacity or stability.
why_possibly_novel: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] Model soups exist for full models; [HYPOTHESIS] soup-vs-rank as a controlled variance-vs-capacity experiment for segmentation PEFT appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 5 domains x data scales {20,200} images: soup-of-4-rank-8 vs rank-32 vs single rank-8, matched compute; verify the two-regime pattern against measured intrinsic ranks.
main_risk: LoRA souping requires compatible subspaces; naive averaging may need alignment (sign/rotation), and the alignment procedure choice affects results.
community_default_belief: Underfitting means insufficient rank; ensembling/averaging is an inference trick orthogonal to PEFT design.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Few-shot + low-rank + init-lottery equals high-variance estimation; classic statistics says averaging attacks exactly that - the community imports capacity intuitions from pretraining into a variance-dominated regime.
fastest_falsification: Six hours: one domain at 20 images, soup vs double-rank.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: LoRA updates are 1-bit compressible: keeping only per-parameter signs (with one learned scale per layer) preserves most adaptation - the knowledge is in directions, not magnitudes.
problem: What information the learned update actually carries (fine-grained magnitudes vs coarse directions) is unknown, though it determines compressibility, mergeability, and how PEFT should be regularized.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Binarizing converged LoRA factors (sign x per-layer scale) retains the large majority of target-domain performance, indicating the update's functional content is directional and low-precision - and predicting that magnitude-focused regularizers and optimizers are tuning noise.
falsifiable_prediction: Sign-binarized LoRAs will retain >80% of adaptation gain across domains; retention will fall as measured intrinsic task rank rises (more information needs more precision); random-sign controls will destroy performance, confirming signs carry the signal.
why_important: 400x adapter compression for deployment fleets; scientifically, quantifies the information content of adaptation (bits per parameter actually used), constraining theories of what fine-tuning learns.
why_possibly_novel: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] Network quantization is mature; [HYPOTHESIS] using extreme quantization as a measurement of adaptation-information content (not just a compression trick) for SAM PEFT appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 6 adapted LoRAs: binarize post-hoc (per-layer optimal scale); evaluate retention; controls: random signs, magnitude-only (sign-shuffled); correlate retention with task intrinsic rank.
main_risk: Post-hoc binarization may need light retraining (QAT-style) to be fair, blurring the pure measurement.
community_default_belief: Learned weights need reasonable precision; adapter compression is an engineering afterthought and magnitudes obviously matter (they're what training optimizes).
why_that_may_be_wrong: If adaptation mostly re-weights existing pathways (W15-B001-A-014), the functional signal is which directions to nudge and which way - a fundamentally low-bit payload.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: binarize one public adapted LoRA, evaluate; <30% retention falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: PEFT's gains arrive almost immediately: most target-domain improvement happens in the first few percent of training steps, and the long tail mainly moves calibration and boundary polish - three separable timescales.
problem: Adaptation training lengths are set by convention (N epochs) with no account of when different capabilities actually change.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] SAM adaptation exhibits distinct timescales: (1) region-level IoU jumps within the first ~5% of steps (convention acquisition), (2) boundary-F improves slowly and linearly, (3) calibration drifts continuously and can worsen late - implying early stopping at timescale-1 completion plus post-hoc head recalibration dominates the standard recipe.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking {region IoU, boundary-F, calibration error} at fine checkpoint resolution across domains will show the three-phase structure with consistent phase boundaries in normalized steps; a stop-at-phase-1 + recalibrate recipe will match full training on region metrics at >10x less compute.
why_important: Compute savings are secondary; the primary yield is a decomposition of WHAT adaptation learns WHEN - conventions vs perception polish vs self-assessment - which informs data needs per phase (few labels suffice for phase 1).
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Fine-grained temporal decomposition of adaptation into capability timescales for promptable segmentation appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 4 domains, dense checkpointing (every 1% of steps), the three metric families; test phase-boundary consistency and the early-stop recipe.
main_risk: Phase structure may be optimizer/schedule-dependent; replicate under 2 schedules to check robustness.
community_default_belief: Adaptation quality accrues gradually over training; train 'to convergence' with the full budget; one final number characterizes the checkpoint.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Different loss components have vastly different gradient magnitudes and data requirements; uniform-progress intuition ignores that convention-fitting is a few-bit problem solved almost instantly by a strong prior.
fastest_falsification: Four hours: one domain, checkpoints at {1,2,5,10,50,100}% of steps, three metrics.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Adaptation without touching the model: a learned 3x3-conv (or LUT) input transformation matches low-rank LoRA on sensor-shift domains - the entire 'domain gap' passes through the lens.
problem: PEFT modifies internals by default; the null hypothesis that many domain gaps are input-space-correctable (photometric, chromatic, noise) is never given a fair trial with learned input transforms.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For sensor/photometric shifts, a tiny learned input-space transform (per-domain color LUT or single conv layer, trained with SAM frozen end-to-end through it) achieves parity with rank-4-8 LoRA - and its learned parameters are interpretable (revealing WHAT the shift physically is).
falsifiable_prediction: On sensor-shift domains, input-transform adaptation will reach >=90% of LoRA-rank-8 gains; on convention-shift domains it will capture near zero - the cleanest gap-typing instrument yet (links W15-B001-A-008/-016); inspecting learned LUTs will recover known physical transformations (e.g., spectral response differences).
why_important: Interpretability of the gap itself (you can read the learned transform), perfect forgetting-safety (base model untouched), and universal composability (works for any model version) - properties no weight-space PEFT offers.
why_possibly_novel: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] Input-space visual prompting/adversarial-reprogramming exists; [HYPOTHESIS] positioning learned input transforms as a gap-typing measurement and parity-class alternative for SAM sensor shifts appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 6 domains (3 sensor-shift, 3 convention-shift): train LUT and 3x3-conv transforms vs LoRA-8; measure parity fractions; inspect transforms against known physics.
main_risk: Some sensor shifts are spatially heterogeneous (vignetting, depth-dependent noise) exceeding LUT expressivity; include a slightly richer transform arm.
community_default_belief: Domain gaps require feature-level correction; input preprocessing is data engineering, not an adaptation method worth benchmarking.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the shift is generated by the imaging pipeline (optics, sensor, compression), its correction lives naturally in input space - the feature-level default is habit, not necessity.
fastest_falsification: Four hours: one thermal/ultrasound domain, LUT vs LoRA-8.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Adaptation by subtraction: learning to GATE (mask out) a small set of encoder channels - adding zero new parameters of representation - recovers much of the domain gap, because shift acts as feature interference.
problem: PEFT universally ADDS capacity; the hypothesis that domain shift mainly ACTIVATES misleading features (which removal would fix) has no direct test.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A learned binary/soft gate over encoder channels (hundreds of parameters) recovers a substantial fraction of LoRA's gains on many domains, because out-of-domain inputs excite feature detectors whose downstream effect is destructive interference rather than missing information.
falsifiable_prediction: Gate-only adaptation will exceed 50% of LoRA-8's gain on a majority of tested domains; gated-off channels will be interpretable (responding to domain-atypical patterns); transplanting the gate to a DIFFERENT adaptation method's base will stack benefits, confirming the interference mechanism is real and separate.
why_important: If subtraction suffices, 'domain gap' is substantially a robustness problem (spurious activation) rather than a knowledge problem - redirecting theory; gates are also trivially mergeable and interpretable, unlike weight deltas.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Channel-gating as a primary adaptation mechanism with the interference interpretation for SAM appears untested (pruning literature targets efficiency, not domain adaptation).
minimal_falsification_experiment: 6 domains: train channel gates (Gumbel or L0-style) with everything else frozen; compare to LoRA-8 and LN-tuning; characterize gated channels' response properties; test gate+LoRA stacking.
main_risk: Gating interacts with LayerNorm statistics; apparent gains might reduce to LN-retuning effects (control needed).
community_default_belief: Adapting means learning new parameters; performance gaps signal missing domain knowledge that added capacity must supply.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A model with universal pretraining plausibly contains the needed features already; its failures may come from actively WRONG features firing - which no additive update can fix as cheaply as removal.
fastest_falsification: Six hours: one domain, gate-only vs LoRA-8; <20% recovery weakens the thesis.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Scale-shifted domains (satellite, microscopy) are adaptable through positional encodings alone: retuning PE frequencies fixes what looks like a semantic gap.
problem: Domains with atypical object-scale statistics show large SAM gaps attributed to content unfamiliarity; the alternative - that the gap is a spatial-frequency prior baked into positional encodings - is untested.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A meaningful share of the zero-shot gap on scale-atypical domains is caused by mismatch between the domain's spatial-structure statistics and the PE's learned/fixed frequency profile; adapting ONLY positional-encoding parameters (a tiny fraction of weights) recovers that share, while content-atypical domains gain nothing from PE tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: PE-only tuning will capture a large fraction of LoRA-8 gains on satellite/microscopy but near zero on content-shifted, scale-typical domains (double dissociation); learned PE changes will show interpretable frequency-profile shifts matching the domain's object-scale spectrum.
why_important: Isolates a specific, interpretable component of 'domain gap' (spatial-statistics prior) from semantic unfamiliarity - conceptually cleaner than monolithic gap narratives, with a near-free adaptation lever.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] PE-only adaptation as a scale-gap isolator for promptable segmentation appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 4 domains (2 scale-shifted, 2 content-shifted): PE-only tuning vs LoRA-8 vs LN-only; spectral analysis of PE changes vs domain scale statistics.
main_risk: SAM's PE implementation details ([KNOWN FACT] it uses learned positional embeddings in the encoder plus random-frequency embeddings for prompts) constrain what 'PE tuning' means; multiple PE-surface variants must be tested.
community_default_belief: Satellite/microscopy gaps reflect unfamiliar content and appearance; scale handling is assumed absorbed by the encoder's general features, and PEs are frozen plumbing nobody adapts.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Object-scale statistics of web photos are narrow; PEs encode spatial priors matched to them, and nothing in standard adaptation diagnoses this separable cause.
fastest_falsification: Six hours: one satellite dataset, PE-only vs LN-only tuning; parity with LN-only (no PE-specific gain) falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Label-free test-time adaptation via self-consistency: a few gradient steps minimizing disagreement across prompts/augmentations of ONE image improves that image's masks - SAM contains its own training signal.
problem: Per-image adaptation at test time is assumed to require labels or source statistics; SAM's promptable interface generates multiple views of the same decision whose agreement is a free, unexploited objective.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Enforcing consistency (via a few LoRA-parameter gradient steps per image) among masks from jittered prompts, flipped inputs, and multimask candidates improves single-image quality on shifted domains, because inconsistency is enriched at exactly the model's error locations (per W15-B001-A-009's premise).
falsifiable_prediction: Per-image consistency optimization will improve IoU on shifted domains by a measurable margin, with gains proportional to pre-adaptation inconsistency (predictable per image); on in-domain images gains will be ~zero (consistency already high) - and failure cases will be 'consistently wrong' images, quantifying that class's prevalence for the first time.
why_important: Deployable label-free adaptation at the single-image level; scientifically, measures how much of SAM's shifted-domain error is 'inconsistency-visible' vs 'confidently wrong' - a fundamental split for all self-supervised adaptation approaches.
why_possibly_novel: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] Test-time training/adaptation exists (classification-focused); [HYPOTHESIS] prompt-consistency as the objective, exploiting promptable-model structure, appears new for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 3 shifted domains: per-image 5-20 step consistency optimization on LoRA params; measure IoU delta vs pre-adaptation inconsistency; ablate consistency-signal components (prompt-jitter vs flip vs multimask).
main_risk: Degenerate solutions (collapse to trivial consistent masks) require careful objective design (e.g., entropy floors) - the engineering could contaminate the scientific claim.
community_default_belief: Test-time adaptation needs batch statistics, source data, or auxiliary tasks; single-image self-supervision for segmentation is considered too weak a signal.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A promptable model is an ensemble in disguise - many prompts, one truth; the disagreement among its own answers is a supervision source unique to this model class and unpriced by classification-era intuitions.
fastest_falsification: Six hours: 100 shifted images, 10-step consistency TTA; zero mean gain (or collapse) falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT
consolidation.mutation_note: MUTATE. SAM + self-consistency test-time adaptation matches the established entropy/consistency-TTA family (method permutation). Salvage: the diagnostic claim that cross-prompt/augmentation inconsistency is spatially enriched at true error locations under shift; test that as a measurement (error-localization AUROC), with per-image adaptation demoted to a secondary intervention arm.

one_line: SAM's self-training ancestry left fingerprints: error modes are correlated across all SAM-derived models because SA-1B was partially machine-generated by earlier SAM versions - a monoculture defect.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] SA-1B's masks were produced with model assistance in progressively automated stages. The population-level consequence - shared blind spots across every model trained on it - is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on SA-1B (SAM variants, distilled/efficient SAMs, and fine-tuned derivatives) share error modes far beyond what architecture or scale predicts - their errors correlate more with each other than with models trained on human-only masks, because the annotation bootstrap propagated specific systematic omissions/conventions.
falsifiable_prediction: Pairwise error correlation between SA-1B-trained models will significantly exceed correlation between an SA-1B model and a human-mask-trained model at matched accuracy; the shared-error set will be enriched in identifiable pattern families (thin structures, transparency, granularity conventions).
why_important: Ensemble/verification pipelines assume model diversity buys independence; a data-lineage monoculture silently breaks that assumption across the entire SAM ecosystem - directly relevant to safety-critical deployments using redundancy arguments.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Data-lineage error-correlation auditing for segmentation foundation ecosystems appears unstudied (related ideas exist for LLM synthetic data, making this a timely cross-pollination).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble {2-3 SA-1B-lineage models, 2 human-data models} at comparable accuracy on neutral benchmarks; compute pairwise error correlations and shared-error taxonomies; control for architecture overlap.
main_risk: Finding comparable-accuracy human-data-trained promptable models is hard; may require training one, raising cost.
community_default_belief: Different checkpoints/architectures provide meaningfully independent opinions; dataset lineage is not tracked as a correlation source in segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Machine-in-the-loop annotation transfers the annotating model's decision boundary into the labels; every downstream learner then inherits correlated blind spots that accuracy metrics never expose.
fastest_falsification: One day: SAM vs one distilled-SAM vs one human-data model on 500 images; lineage-independent correlation structure falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: SAM carries a masks-per-image prior: everything-mode output counts regress toward SA-1B's per-image mask-count distribution regardless of true scene content.
problem: Whether generative-style dataset priors (how many things a scene 'should' contain) leak into a promptable discriminative model is unknown but consequential for counting and coverage uses.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On synthetic scenes with controlled true object counts spanning 1 to thousands, SAM's everything-mode count deviates from truth systematically TOWARD the SA-1B per-image mask-count mode, beyond what grid/NMS mechanics (W15-B001-A-040) explain - i.e., a learned prior in the decoder/IoU-filtering, not just sampling mechanics.
falsifiable_prediction: After correcting for the grid+NMS model's predicted counts, residual deviations will still point toward the SA-1B modal count; manipulating only IoU-threshold filtering won't remove the pull; the pull will be strongest for scenes most unlike web photos.
why_important: Separates mechanical from learned components of a dataset prior - methodologically valuable - and warns quantitative users (cell counting, inventory) of a content-independent bias with a measurable direction.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Testing for learned count priors in promptable segmentation, distinct from sampler mechanics, appears novel.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetic count sweeps (10 scene styles x counts 1..1000); fit mechanical model; test residual pull toward SA-1B statistics ([KNOWN FACT] SA-1B averages on the order of 100 masks/image per its release description); vary filtering thresholds.
main_risk: The mechanical model must be very good or residuals are meaningless; requires careful validation on scenes where no prior conflict exists.
community_default_belief: Everything-mode output is determined by image content plus sampler settings; the model has no opinion about how many objects exist.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The IoU head and mask-ranking machinery were trained under a specific count regime; density-dependent score calibration is a cheap shortcut SGD would exploit, creating an implicit count prior.
fastest_falsification: Six hours: two extreme-count synthetic scenes, mechanical-model residuals; zero systematic pull falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: 'Segment anything' has measurable anisotropy: zero-shot quality stratified by scene type maps SA-1B's content skew, quantifying WHERE the anything-claim fails before any domain-specific study.
problem: SAM's generality is asserted via aggregate benchmarks; a systematic scene-type-stratified capability map, tied quantitatively to pretraining content distribution, does not exist.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Zero-shot performance across scene taxonomies (indoor/outdoor, aerial, document, industrial, scientific imaging, etc.) varies widely and correlates strongly with content-frequency estimates in SA-1B-like web-photo distributions - making 'domain gap' largely predictable from content frequency rather than intrinsic difficulty.
falsifiable_prediction: A frequency-based predictor (estimated from a public SA-1B sample or a proxy web-photo distribution) will explain a large share of variance in stratified zero-shot IoU; difficulty-matched comparisons (same object complexity, different frequency) will still show the frequency effect - dissociating rarity from hardness.
why_important: Converts anecdotal 'SAM fails on X' into a predictive capability atlas; identifies underserved strata for the next pretraining round; provides adaptation-need forecasts for new applications from frequency lookups alone.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] A frequency-vs-difficulty dissociated capability atlas for SAM appears unbuilt; existing evaluations catalog performance without the pretraining-distribution linkage.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 20 scene strata x matched prompt protocol; estimate stratum frequencies from an SA-1B sample; regress stratified IoU on frequency with difficulty covariates (object size, boundary complexity, contrast).
main_risk: Frequency estimation for strata is noisy; use multiple proxy corpora and report sensitivity.
community_default_belief: SAM generalizes broadly with a few known weak spots (medical, camouflage); failures are attributed to intrinsic domain difficulty rather than pretraining exposure statistics.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Difficulty and rarity are conflated in every existing evaluation; models fail on the rare more than the hard, but no segmentation study has separated the two axes.
fastest_falsification: One day: 6 strata with frequency estimates; no frequency-IoU relationship after difficulty controls falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: SAM inherited photographic curation: at matched scene content and difficulty, 'non-photogenic' captures (bad framing, defocus, clutter) segment worse than curated-style photos - an aesthetics bias in a geometry model.
problem: Web-scraped pretraining images pass aesthetic/curation filters; whether this biases a segmentation model against ordinary uncurated captures (surveillance, robotics, user snapshots) is untested.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Holding scene content constant, SAM performs measurably worse on uncurated-style captures than curated-style captures of the SAME scenes, beyond what image-quality metrics explain - because composition statistics (centering, lighting, depth-of-field conventions) are themselves features SAM's grouping relies on.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired captures (same scene, tripod-curated vs casual framing/exposure), IoU will favor curated systematically; the gap will persist after matching sharpness/exposure metrics; encoder features of casual captures will be measurably closer to SAM's low-performance strata.
why_important: Robotics/AR/surveillance consume uncurated frames; a curation bias means benchmark numbers (built from curated photos) systematically overstate field performance - a deployment-relevant, quantifiable correction.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Isolating curation/composition bias via same-scene paired captures for segmentation appears undone (related biases are studied for image aesthetics, not for grouping ability).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect ~200 scene pairs (curated vs casual capture of identical scenes); annotate shared objects; evaluate SAM under matched prompts; regress the gap on quality covariates to isolate the composition effect.
main_risk: Collecting genuinely content-matched pairs is labor-intensive; existing multi-view datasets may partially substitute.
community_default_belief: Segmentation robustness is about corruption/noise; 'framing style' is not recognized as a performance factor for geometry-level tasks.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Curated photos have statistical regularities (subject centering, background separation via depth-of-field) that make grouping easier AND were the training distribution - a compounding advantage invisible to corruption benchmarks.
fastest_falsification: Six hours with an existing multi-view/casual-capture dataset: gap after quality matching; zero gap falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Active learning driven by SAM's IoU head selects convention conflicts, not model errors: the head's 'low quality' flags concentrate where target-domain labeling conventions differ from SA-1B's, wasting annotation budget.
problem: The IoU head is trained to predict overlap with SA-1B-convention masks; when used to drive data selection in a new domain, what it actually flags is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In convention-mismatched domains, low-predicted-IoU instances are enriched in convention disagreements (model produces an SA-1B-style valid mask that the target convention scores poorly) rather than perception failures; annotation budget spent there teaches the convention repeatedly instead of fixing errors - explaining observed inefficiency of confidence-based AL for SAM.
falsifiable_prediction: Manual coding of low-predicted-IoU selections will show convention-conflict enrichment vs random selections; an AL loop that first learns the convention from 5 labels then re-scores will redirect selections toward genuine errors and improve label efficiency measurably.
why_important: Explains and fixes a concrete AL pathology; sharpens the general principle that self-assessment transfers WORSE than skill across conventions - important as more pipelines trust foundation-model confidence signals.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] The convention-conflict account of confidence-driven AL failure for SAM, with the two-stage fix, appears unarticulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 2 convention-mismatched domains: code 100 low-confidence selections into {conflict, error, noise}; run AL with {confidence, convention-corrected confidence, random}; compare efficiency curves.
main_risk: Coding conflict-vs-error requires clear convention documentation for the target domain; ambiguous cases could blur enrichment statistics.
community_default_belief: Low predicted quality marks where the model needs help; AL with model confidence is a sensible default for foundation-model adaptation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: 'Quality' was defined by the pretraining convention; under convention shift the head measures disagreement-with-SA-1B-style, which is maximal exactly where the target convention differs - not where the model fails.
fastest_falsification: Four hours: code 50 low-confidence flags in one medical domain; no conflict enrichment falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Privacy blurring in SA-1B taught SAM that blur boundaries are object boundaries: synthetic blur patches attract spurious masks at rates exceeding matched smooth regions.
problem: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] SA-1B images had faces and license plates blurred for privacy per its release documentation. Whether models learn these processing artifacts as segmentation cues is unknown.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because blurred regions in SA-1B co-occurred with maskable objects (faces, plates), SAM learned blur-transition edges as objectness evidence; it will therefore segment synthetic Gaussian-blur patches as objects at above-baseline rates, and be biased toward mask boundaries that follow blur transitions in natural defocus.
falsifiable_prediction: Everything-mode and point prompts on images with inserted blur patches (vs luminance-matched smooth patches) will produce masks aligned to blur boundaries significantly more often; the effect will scale with blur-kernel similarity to privacy-blur styles.
why_important: A concrete, checkable instance of preprocessing-artifact learning in foundation datasets - a contamination class that generalizes (watermarks, compression, resize artifacts) and matters for any dataset built with automated redaction.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Testing privacy-redaction artifacts as learned segmentation cues appears novel; artifact learning is documented for classification shortcuts but not for promptable segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert blur patches and matched controls into 500 natural images at random locations; measure mask-attraction rates and boundary-alignment; sweep kernel types; compare against a human-data-trained model as lineage control.
main_risk: Blur patches differ from controls in multiple statistics; constructing fair 'equally salient but not blur' controls is the crux.
community_default_belief: Dataset preprocessing (redaction, resizing) is content-neutral plumbing; models learn objects, not pipeline artifacts, especially for geometric tasks.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Redaction is spatially correlated with exactly the high-value mask regions (faces/plates ARE objects), creating a strong learnable association between the artifact and the label - textbook shortcut-learning conditions.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 100 images with blur vs control patches, attraction-rate comparison.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: SA-1B is massively redundant for capability: models trained on well-chosen small fractions recover most zero-shot segmentation ability - measurable at reduced scale, with implications for what pretraining actually needs.
problem: The relationship between SA-1B's scale ([KNOWN FACT] ~11M images / ~1.1B masks per its release description) and SAM's capabilities is unquantified; nobody knows the capability-per-datum curve or its shape.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Capability saturates far below full scale under diversity-preserving subsampling: at compact model scale, training on a low-single-digit percent subset selected for scene/mask-statistics coverage recovers the large majority of full-subset-trained zero-shot performance, while random subsets need several times more data - implying capability lives in coverage, not count.
falsifiable_prediction: Capability-vs-fraction curves (at fixed small architecture) will show early saturation for coverage-selected subsets and a persistent coverage-vs-random gap; the gap will be largest on rare-strata evaluations (linking W15-B001-A-087).
why_important: Pretraining-data economics for the segmentation-foundation era: if coverage dominates count, the next SAM-class model can be trained dramatically cheaper, and dataset releases should prioritize strata balance over volume - a testable, consequential claim.
why_possibly_novel: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] Data pruning/coreset results exist for classification pretraining; [HYPOTHESIS] capability-curve measurement for promptable-segmentation pretraining appears unattempted publicly.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fixed compact promptable architecture; train on {0.5,1,2,5,10}% SA-1B subsets x {random, coverage-selected}; evaluate zero-shot on a stratified suite; fit and compare capability curves.
main_risk: Conclusions at compact scale may not extrapolate to ViT-H scale; frame claims as scale-conditional with scaling-trend checks at 2 model sizes.
community_default_belief: SAM's generality comes from its billion-mask scale; 'more data' is the assumed ingredient behind zero-shot breadth.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Web-scale collections are internally redundant (near-duplicate scenes, correlated content); effective information may be orders of magnitude smaller than raw counts - demonstrated repeatedly in other modalities and never tested here.
fastest_falsification: Multi-day but bounded: 1% coverage vs 1% random at tiny scale; no coverage advantage anywhere falsifies the interesting half.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: The ultrasound gap is mostly speckle, not anatomy: augmenting natural images with physically-modeled speckle noise closes a large share of SAM's ultrasound deficit without a single ultrasound image.
problem: Ultrasound is treated as a semantically alien domain requiring in-domain data; the alternative decomposition - that the gap is dominated by low-level speckle statistics disrupting SAM's edge machinery - is untested.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A LoRA trained ONLY on natural images corrupted with simulated speckle (multiplicative Rayleigh-family noise, no anatomy content) will transfer to real ultrasound and recover a large fraction of the gain achieved by training on real ultrasound - because the binding constraint is noise-statistics robustness, not anatomical knowledge.
falsifiable_prediction: Speckle-only adaptation will achieve a substantial fraction (predicted >50%) of real-data adaptation gains on ultrasound benchmarks; residual gaps will concentrate in convention-dependent structures (measurement standards) rather than boundary-finding failures.
why_important: Decomposes a major modality gap into transferable-physics vs domain-knowledge components; validates a data-free adaptation path for any speckle modality (OCT, SAR share the noise family [KNOWN FACT]) - the recipe generalizes if the decomposition holds.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Physics-only augmentation as a quantitative gap-decomposition instrument (not just an augmentation trick) for SAM-to-ultrasound appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train LoRA on speckle-augmented natural images; evaluate on 3 ultrasound datasets vs {zero-shot, real-data LoRA}; decompose residual errors into boundary vs convention types.
main_risk: Speckle simulation fidelity matters; if simple models fail, the negative result conflates decomposition-wrongness with simulator-wrongness (include 2 simulator fidelity levels).
community_default_belief: Medical modality gaps require in-domain training data; ultrasound especially is considered visually sui generis, demanding anatomy-aware adaptation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: SAM's grouping machinery is edge-driven (see W15-B001-A-038); speckle specifically destroys edge statistics, so restoring robustness to that one corruption may be most of what 'ultrasound adaptation' actually learns.
fastest_falsification: One day: speckle-LoRA vs zero-shot on one ultrasound set; no improvement falsifies immediately.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Histopathology breaks SAM through scale-lessness, not appearance: without absolute-scale cues its granularity choice becomes unstable, and instability (not inaccuracy) is the measurable failure mode.
problem: SAM's poor histopathology performance is attributed to appearance shift (stains, textures); an alternative - that scale-free self-similar content destabilizes granularity selection - makes different predictions nobody has separated.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Pathology tiles lack the absolute-scale cues (familiar objects, perspective) that SAM implicitly uses for granularity selection; consequently, SAM's outputs on pathology are hypersensitive to zoom level and prompt position (unstable), even where per-prompt masks are locally plausible - instability is the primary defect, distinct from and larger than appearance-driven inaccuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Across magnifications of the same tissue, mask granularity will jump erratically (low cross-scale consistency) compared with natural images under equivalent rescaling; injecting artificial scale cues (a rendered scale bar or reference object) will measurably stabilize granularity - a signature no appearance-gap account predicts.
why_important: Redefines what pathology adaptation must fix (stabilize scale selection, not just restyle features), suggesting scale-conditioning as the key intervention; contributes a clean instance of 'missing context cue' failure in foundation models.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] The scale-cue-dependence of SAM's granularity selection, and instability-vs-inaccuracy decomposition for pathology, appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-magnification pathology tiles + rescaled natural-image controls: measure cross-scale mask consistency; test scale-cue injection; decompose errors into instability vs inaccuracy components.
main_risk: Scale-bar injection is unusual input that may cause its own artifacts; needs multiple cue types (text magnification labels, reference objects) for convergent evidence.
community_default_belief: Pathology is hard for SAM because of extreme appearance shift (stains, cellular textures unlike web photos); the fix is in-domain fine-tuning on stained tissue.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Local mask plausibility on pathology is often decent - the errors look like wrong-level-of-organization choices (cell vs gland vs region), which is a scale-selection pathology, not a perception pathology.
fastest_falsification: Six hours: cross-magnification consistency on 50 tiles vs natural controls; equal stability falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Geometry beats appearance in clutter: SAM segments rendered depth maps better than the corresponding RGB in dense scenes - though depth was near-absent from its training data.
problem: Which input representation best exposes objects to SAM's grouping machinery is untested; the default assumption (RGB, its training modality) may fail in clutter where texture misleads.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For cluttered scenes, depth maps rendered as grayscale expose occlusion boundaries so cleanly that zero-shot SAM segments objects better from depth than from RGB - implying SAM's grouping is substantially a generic contour engine whose performance is input-representation-limited, not knowledge-limited, in clutter.
falsifiable_prediction: On RGB-D benchmarks' cluttered subsets, depth-input SAM will beat RGB-input SAM on instance-level metrics; fusion (min-cost of both) will beat either, and the depth advantage will correlate with a clutter/texture-conflict measure - vanishing on clean scenes.
why_important: Practical: robots with depth sensors get better segmentation for free by feeding the 'wrong' modality; scientific: quantifies how much of SAM is transferable contour-machinery vs RGB-specific knowledge - informing what future promptable models should train on.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Zero-shot cross-representation superiority (depth beating native RGB in identifiable regimes) appears undocumented; depth-SAM work focuses on fusing, not on the counterintuitive comparison.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 2 RGB-D datasets stratified by clutter: SAM on {RGB, normalized depth, surface-normal rendering}; instance metrics per stratum; correlate depth advantage with clutter scores.
main_risk: Depth rendering choices (normalization, hole filling) strongly affect results; must standardize and report sensitivity.
community_default_belief: SAM should be fed the modality it was trained on; depth is an auxiliary channel requiring fusion architectures or fine-tuning to exploit.
why_that_may_be_wrong: SAM's edge-driven grouping (W15-B001-A-038) doesn't care what the intensity gradient MEANS; depth discontinuities are more veridical object boundaries than reflectance edges - in clutter, the training-modality prior may be a handicap.
fastest_falsification: Four hours: 100 cluttered RGB-D frames, both inputs; RGB winning everywhere falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Structure supervises better than labels: adapting SAM to CT using ONLY inter-slice mask-consistency (no annotations) beats few-shot LoRA - volumetric coherence is a free supervisory signal labels can't match.
problem: Volumetric medical adaptation defaults to slice-level supervised fine-tuning; the unlabeled 3D structure of the data (adjacent slices must have coherent masks) is discarded as a training signal.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Enforcing prompt-propagated consistency between adjacent CT slices (segment slice i with a prompt, derive prompts for i+1 from the result, penalize incoherence) provides enough signal to adapt LoRA parameters label-free, and outperforms 10-20-image supervised LoRA - because it supplies thousands of weak constraints vs dozens of strong ones targeting exactly the model's instability modes.
falsifiable_prediction: Consistency-trained LoRA will beat few-shot supervised LoRA on held-out labeled CT across organs, with gains concentrated on structures where zero-shot SAM is inconsistent across slices (predictable a priori); combining both will be superadditive on small budgets.
why_important: Label-free volumetric adaptation would remove the annotation bottleneck for 3D medical deployment; conceptually tests whether coherence constraints (physics/geometry of the data) can substitute for semantic supervision - a question relevant to video and multi-view too.
why_possibly_novel: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] Slice-propagation inference schemes for SAM on volumes exist; [HYPOTHESIS] using propagation coherence as a TRAINING objective for label-free PEFT appears distinct and untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 2 CT datasets: consistency-only LoRA vs {zero-shot, 10-shot, 20-shot supervised LoRA}; evaluate on labeled volumes; ablate consistency-loss components; check degenerate-solution controls.
main_risk: Consistency has trivial optima (empty/full masks propagate perfectly); objective needs anti-collapse terms whose design could dominate outcomes.
community_default_belief: Adaptation requires labels; unlabeled target data helps only via weak tricks (pseudo-labels, statistics alignment) that underperform even few-shot supervision.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Volumes provide near-ground-truth constraints for free (anatomy is continuous); a few labeled slices carry conventions but cannot cover instability modes, which are exactly what dense weak constraints regularize.
fastest_falsification: One day: consistency-only vs 10-shot on one organ; supervised winning decisively falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: SAM has an orientation prior from photography: rotation-sweep evaluation reveals anisotropic segmentation quality, and remote-sensing 'domain gap' partly dissolves under test-time rotation averaging.
problem: Natural photos have canonical orientation (gravity down, horizons horizontal); how much orientation prior SAM absorbed, and its contribution to overhead-imagery gaps, is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] SAM's quality on the same object varies systematically with its orientation (best at photo-canonical orientations); overhead imagery - which lacks canonical orientation - pays this anisotropy as a permanent tax that rotation-averaged inference (or PE-level fixes, W15-B001-A-083) largely removes without any training.
falsifiable_prediction: Rotation sweeps on natural objects will show quality oscillation with consistent phase (axis-aligned peaks); satellite benchmarks will gain measurably from 4-fold or 8-fold rotation-averaged inference while natural benchmarks gain little; anisotropy magnitude will predict per-dataset rotation-averaging gains.
why_important: A zero-training improvement for the entire remote-sensing SAM ecosystem plus a clean measurement of an inductive bias everyone suspects and nobody has quantified for promptable segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Orientation-anisotropy quantification for SAM with the rotation-averaging causal test appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rotation sweeps (0-360 in 15-degree steps) on 300 natural + 300 overhead instances with rotation-corrected prompts; measure anisotropy spectra; test rotation-averaged inference on 2 satellite benchmarks.
main_risk: Rotation introduces interpolation artifacts and boundary-truncation confounds; needs padding/crop protocols that isolate the orientation effect.
community_default_belief: Overhead-imagery gaps are about content (roofs, fields unlike web photos) and resolution; orientation handling is assumed adequate because convolutions/attention have no explicit orientation dependence.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Learned features inherit dataset statistics regardless of architectural symmetry - photographic orientation regularity is strong, and no mechanism removes it; the community conflates architectural equivariance with learned invariance.
fastest_falsification: Four hours: rotation sweep on 100 natural objects; flat quality-vs-angle falsifies.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: LoRAs die with their base model - but a cheap linear re-basing transform resurrects them: adapter knowledge is basis-specific yet linearly portable across model versions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] SAM 2 uses a different image encoder (Hiera-based) than SAM's ViT. Organizations hold growing libraries of domain LoRAs that become worthless on model upgrades; whether adapter knowledge is portable across versions is unstudied.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A domain LoRA's function can be transported to a new base model by learning a small linear map between the two models' feature spaces (fit on unlabeled generic images) and re-projecting the update - recovering a large fraction of adaptation quality without target-domain data, because the update encodes a feature-space displacement that survives linear re-expression.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-based LoRAs will recover >50% of from-scratch adaptation gains on the new model across domains; recovery will correlate with the linearity of the inter-model feature correspondence (measurable via CKA of the fitted map's residuals) - identifying when re-basing is trustworthy.
why_important: Adapter portability determines the economics of foundation-model upgrades ecosystem-wide; scientifically, tests whether adaptation knowledge is a basis-independent object (a 'domain vector') or entangled with model internals - a fundamental representation question.
why_possibly_novel: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] Cross-model representation alignment (linear-mapping studies) exists; [HYPOTHESIS] operationalizing it to transplant PEFT updates across segmentation model generations appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 3 domain LoRAs on SAM: fit linear stitching maps SAM->SAM2-encoder on unlabeled images; transport updates; evaluate vs {zero-shot SAM2, from-scratch SAM2 LoRA}; correlate recovery with map residuals.
main_risk: Architectural mismatch (attention layout, resolution hierarchy) may make per-layer correspondence ill-defined; may require transporting at feature-interface level (encoder output) only.
community_default_belief: Adapters are throwaway artifacts bound to one checkpoint; upgrades mean re-collecting data or re-training everything - portability isn't even attempted.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Different models trained on similar data develop linearly-relatable representations (a recurring empirical finding); if so, updates - which live in representation space - should be relatable by the same maps.
fastest_falsification: One day: one LoRA, encoder-output-level transport, one domain; near-zero recovery falsifies the linear-portability form.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Adaptation is path-dependent: fine-tuning A-then-B lands somewhere different from B-then-A even with identical final data exposure - sequential PEFT composes non-commutatively with predictable asymmetry.
problem: Real deployments adapt models repeatedly (new sites, new sensors); whether adaptation order matters - and which orders are better - has no established answer for segmentation PEFT.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Sequential LoRA adaptation (training one adapter through domains in sequence) is non-commutative: final joint performance depends on order, with a predictable rule - adapting from broad/diverse domains toward narrow ones preserves more joint capability than the reverse, because narrow-first commits shared directions to domain-specific uses (relates to W15-B001-A-031's capacity pressure).
falsifiable_prediction: For domain pairs (broad, narrow): broad-first order will yield better average performance across both domains than narrow-first, beyond seed noise; the asymmetry magnitude will correlate with measured update-subspace overlap between the two domains (linking W15-B001-A-022); joint (mixed) training will bound both orders.
why_important: Deployment guidance for continual adaptation (order your rollout curriculum) and a probe of PEFT's loss-landscape geometry - non-commutativity constrains theories that model adaptation as reaching a data-defined optimum independent of path.
why_possibly_novel: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK] Task-order effects are studied in continual learning generally; [HYPOTHESIS] the broad-to-narrow rule with subspace-overlap prediction for segmentation PEFT appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 4 domain pairs varying breadth contrast x both orders x 3 seeds, matched total steps; measure joint performance asymmetry; regress on subspace overlap and breadth measures.
main_risk: 'Breadth' needs an operational definition (feature-space dispersion); a bad proxy could bury a real effect.
community_default_belief: With the same total data, adaptation reaches roughly the same place; order effects are second-order noise handled by replay buffers if at all.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Low-rank adapters have scarce capacity; early tasks structurally claim subspaces (B=0 symmetry breaking, W15-B001-A-013) that later tasks must work around - a mechanism absent from full fine-tuning intuitions the field borrows.
fastest_falsification: One day: one high-contrast pair, both orders, 3 seeds; symmetric outcomes falsify.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT

one_line: Domain routing is already solved inside the frozen encoder: nearest-centroid gating on SAM features routes multi-domain traffic to the right LoRA as accurately as oracle domain labels - deployment needs no trained router.
problem: Serving many domain LoRAs requires knowing which to apply per image; trained routers add components and fail silently on novel domains - whether frozen features suffice for routing is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Domain identity is so linearly separable in frozen SAM encoder features that a training-free router (nearest domain-centroid, centroids from ~20 unlabeled images each) matches oracle-label routing end-to-end, and its distance-to-nearest-centroid doubles as a calibrated novel-domain detector triggering fallback to zero-shot mode.
falsifiable_prediction: Routing accuracy across 10 domains will exceed 99% with 20-shot centroids; end-to-end IoU under learned routing will be within noise of oracle routing; centroid-distance thresholds will detect held-out novel domains with high AUROC - all with zero trained parameters.
why_important: Removes a whole component class from multi-domain deployment (with its training data, failure modes, maintenance), and quantifies how much 'domain' information the encoder exposes for free - relevant to routing questions across all foundation-model serving.
why_possibly_novel: [HYPOTHESIS] Training-free adapter routing with integrated novelty fallback, validated end-to-end for segmentation serving, appears unreported; MoE-style routing literature assumes trained gates.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 10 domains with LoRAs: build 20-shot centroids; measure routing accuracy, end-to-end IoU vs oracle, and novelty detection on 3 held-out domains; stress-test near-duplicate domains (e.g., two CT sites).
main_risk: Fine-grained domain pairs (same modality, different sites) may collide in feature space - exactly where routing matters clinically; the stress test is the real hypothesis test.
community_default_belief: Mixture/routing systems need learned gating; unsupervised feature clustering is too coarse for production routing across similar domains.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Encoder features encode acquisition characteristics (sensor, protocol) extremely strongly - often MORE strongly than semantics (a common observation in transfer learning) - making domain routing the easy case, not the hard one.
fastest_falsification: Four hours: centroid routing over 5 available domains including 2 similar ones; sub-95% accuracy on the similar pair falsifies the strong claim.

consolidation.territory: T01 SAM / Foundation Model adaptation / PEFT
consolidation.mutation_note: MUTATE. 'Frozen features separate domains' is a widely assumed premise and nearest-centroid routing is engineering assembly. Salvage: rewrite around the only non-obvious content - the failure boundary on near-duplicate domains (e.g. two CT sites) and whether centroid distance is a calibrated novel-domain detector.

one_line: For mature organ benchmarks, the residual model-vs-reference gap is annotation protocol disagreement, not model error.
problem: Benchmarks report residual Dice gaps that drive method development, but it is unknown how much of that gap is achievable at all given rater disagreement.
core_hypothesis: On well-benchmarked large organs, top models already sit inside the inter-rater disagreement band; the residual gap measures protocol ambiguity rather than model deficiency.
falsifiable_prediction: With fresh multi-rater re-annotation of an existing organ test set, model-vs-rater disagreement will be statistically indistinguishable from rater-vs-rater disagreement for a majority of large organs.
why_important: If true, continued leaderboard chasing on these organs is measurement noise, and effort should shift to protocol standardization and genuinely unsolved structures.
why_possibly_novel: Inter-rater variability is often reported descriptively, but the specific null hypothesis that a trained model is an exchangeable rater on existing benchmarks is rarely tested formally.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select one public abdominal CT organ test set; obtain three independent expert re-annotations of about 30 cases; run equivalence tests comparing model-rater versus rater-rater Dice and surface distance distributions.
main_risk: Expert re-annotation is costly, and ambiguity may be organ-specific, weakening any general claim.
community_default_belief: Residual benchmark gaps reflect model limitations that better architectures or training will close.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Reference masks are single-rater products of ambiguous protocols, so the target itself carries irreducible variance that bounds achievable scores.
fastest_falsification: If model-rater disagreement significantly exceeds rater-rater disagreement on most re-annotated organs, the hypothesis is false.

one_line: Boundary label noise in 3D medical data is anisotropic and systematic because annotators trace in-plane, and models inherit a slice-direction-dependent boundary bias.
problem: Label noise in volumetric segmentation is usually modeled as isotropic random perturbation, ignoring how annotation is physically performed slice by slice.
core_hypothesis: Out-of-plane (through-slice) boundary labels are systematically biased and noisier than in-plane boundaries, and trained models reproduce this anisotropic error pattern.
falsifiable_prediction: Surface error of both labels and model predictions, decomposed by surface-normal direction, will be significantly larger for surfaces normal to the acquisition axis, and retraining on reoriented volumes will rotate the error pattern accordingly.
why_important: Anisotropic label bias corrupts volumetry and margin decisions in a directionally structured way that isotropic noise-robust methods cannot fix.
why_possibly_novel: Noise-robust segmentation work typically assumes direction-independent noise; a directional decomposition of label error tied to annotation mechanics is rarely the object of study.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a dataset with near-isotropic voxels, compare per-surface-normal boundary disagreement between two rater sets; train identical models on axial versus reformatted coronal annotations and test whether error anisotropy follows the annotation plane.
main_risk: Anisotropic acquisition resolution confounds annotation-plane effects; needs isotropic data to separate the two.
community_default_belief: Label noise is approximately random and can be averaged out with enough data or noise-robust losses.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Annotation is a physical in-plane act; its errors are structured by the viewing plane and are learned as systematic bias, not variance.
fastest_falsification: If boundary error shows no dependence on surface orientation relative to the annotation plane on isotropic data, the hypothesis fails.

one_line: Annotator identity is decodable from masks alone, and annotator-style normalization improves cross-dataset transfer more than image harmonization.
problem: Cross-dataset segmentation transfer is treated as an image-domain problem, while systematic differences in who drew the labels are ignored.
core_hypothesis: Each annotator or annotating institution has a stable, learnable contouring style (margin tightness, smoothing, inclusion rules), and this style is a first-order component of cross-dataset performance gaps.
falsifiable_prediction: A classifier will predict annotator or source institution from mask geometry alone well above chance, and style-conditioning or style-normalizing labels will recover a substantial share of the cross-dataset Dice drop without touching the images.
why_important: If label style, not image appearance, drives much of the domain gap, the field is optimizing the wrong pipeline stage with image harmonization and domain adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: Rater bias is known in quality-assurance literature, but treating contouring style as a transferable, conditionable variable inside segmentation training is not standard practice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On any dataset with per-rater metadata, train a mask-only rater classifier; then train a segmentation model with a rater-conditioning token and test cross-rater generalization against an unconditioned baseline.
main_risk: Public datasets rarely release annotator identity, limiting where the hypothesis can be tested.
community_default_belief: Cross-dataset gaps are caused mainly by scanner and population shift in the images.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The supervision target changes across datasets too; models fit the labeling function, and different institutions implement different labeling functions.
fastest_falsification: If mask-only classifiers cannot beat chance at identifying the annotating source, style is not a stable learnable signal and the hypothesis collapses.

one_line: Many 3D reference masks are sparse-slice annotations completed by interpolation, and models trained on them learn interpolation artifacts as anatomy.
problem: Dataset construction details such as slice-skipping plus interpolation are undocumented, yet they define the geometry statistics of the ground truth.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on interpolation-completed labels acquire an over-smooth surface prior whose curvature statistics match the interpolation operator rather than true anatomy.
falsifiable_prediction: Surface curvature spectra of model predictions will match interpolated-label statistics and differ measurably from densely annotated reference surfaces of the same organs; training on densely annotated subsets will shift predictions toward higher-frequency surfaces.
why_important: Smoothness that comes from annotation shortcuts silently erases fine anatomical detail relevant for surgical planning and early pathology.
why_possibly_novel: The interpolation step of dataset creation is almost never treated as a bias source with measurable spectral signatures in model outputs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Densely annotate a small set of organs at every slice; compare curvature and surface-frequency statistics between dense labels, interpolated labels, and predictions of models trained on each.
main_risk: True anatomy may genuinely be smooth for many organs, making the effect small except for detailed structures.
community_default_belief: Reference masks represent expert-perceived anatomy at the dataset resolution.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Annotation economics force sparse tracing; the completion operator, not the expert, decides fine-scale geometry.
fastest_falsification: If model surface statistics are indistinguishable between dense-trained and interpolated-trained versions, the artifact-learning claim fails.

one_line: Label errors concentrate at pathology and low-contrast interfaces, so uniform-noise-robust training fails precisely where errors are clinically costly.
problem: Noise-robust segmentation methods are validated with synthetic uniform or random-boundary noise, but real annotation errors are input-dependent.
core_hypothesis: Real label error rate is a strong function of local image evidence (contrast, pathology presence), and methods tuned on uniform synthetic noise select for exactly the wrong robustness mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: A map of rater disagreement will correlate strongly with local contrast and pathology masks; noise-robust methods that win under synthetic uniform noise will show no advantage, or a disadvantage, under real multi-rater noise in low-contrast regions.
why_important: Method rankings from synthetic-noise benchmarks may be anti-predictive for clinical robustness where errors matter most.
why_possibly_novel: The mismatch between synthetic noise models and spatially structured, evidence-dependent real annotation noise is rarely quantified head-to-head for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use any multi-rater dataset to build an empirical noise model conditioned on local contrast; re-evaluate two or three published noise-robust training schemes under empirical versus uniform noise and compare rank stability.
main_risk: Empirical noise models require multi-rater data, and conclusions may not transfer across modalities.
community_default_belief: Robustness to injected random label noise implies robustness to real annotation noise.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Real noise is correlated with image difficulty, so it shifts decision boundaries systematically instead of adding variance the model can average out.
fastest_falsification: If rater disagreement shows no meaningful correlation with local contrast or pathology, the structured-noise premise is wrong.

one_line: Training on raw per-rater masks as separate supervision samples yields calibrated boundary uncertainty for free, beating post-hoc uncertainty methods.
problem: Multi-rater annotations are usually fused into a single consensus mask before training, discarding the disagreement structure that clinical users actually need.
core_hypothesis: A vanilla segmentation network trained on unfused per-rater masks converges to the empirical rater distribution at boundaries, providing spatial uncertainty that matches held-out rater disagreement better than ensembles or MC-dropout applied to consensus-trained models.
falsifiable_prediction: On held-out multi-rater cases, softmax probabilities of the rater-sampled model will match empirical rater agreement fractions more closely (lower calibration error against rater distribution) than ensemble or dropout uncertainty from consensus training.
why_important: It would provide clinically meaningful ambiguity maps without any specialized probabilistic machinery, changing default practice for multi-rater data.
why_possibly_novel: Probabilistic segmentation research focuses on dedicated generative or ensemble architectures; the simple baseline of not fusing raters is rarely evaluated as the primary uncertainty method against them.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one multi-rater dataset, train the same architecture on consensus masks versus rater-sampled masks; compare voxelwise predicted probability to held-out rater agreement fractions.
main_risk: With few raters per case the empirical distribution is coarse and the learned probabilities may be poorly resolved.
community_default_belief: Consensus fusion improves label quality, and uncertainty should be added by dedicated probabilistic methods afterwards.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Fusion destroys exactly the signal uncertainty methods try to reconstruct; keeping raters separate preserves it in the loss directly.
fastest_falsification: If the rater-sampled model's probabilities fit held-out rater disagreement no better than consensus-trained ensembles, the free-calibration claim is false.

one_line: Annotation guidelines drift during a labeling campaign, so early versus late cases in one dataset differ systematically and are temporally decodable.
problem: Datasets are treated as internally homogeneous, but labeling campaigns run for months while conventions are being clarified.
core_hypothesis: Within a single dataset, annotation date (or case index as its proxy) predicts systematic mask differences, and models fit an average of shifting conventions rather than a single labeling function.
falsifiable_prediction: A classifier will distinguish early-campaign from late-campaign masks above chance from mask geometry; splitting train and test by campaign time will show a within-dataset generalization gap absent in random splits.
why_important: Within-dataset protocol drift inflates apparent model error and contaminates any analysis that assumes exchangeable labels.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal ordering of annotation is essentially never analyzed as a variance component in segmentation datasets.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain any dataset with annotation timestamps or sequential case ids; test mask-feature drift over time and compare temporal-split versus random-split evaluation of a fixed model.
main_risk: Timestamps are rarely published; case ordering may correlate with clinical case-mix changes rather than protocol drift.
community_default_belief: A curated dataset represents one consistent labeling protocol.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Protocols are living documents; ambiguity resolutions accumulate during a campaign and change what annotators draw.
fastest_falsification: If no temporal signal in mask statistics exists after controlling for case-mix, the drift hypothesis fails for that dataset.

one_line: Much boundary disagreement is ontological, not perceptual: raters disagree about anatomical definitions, and per-region definition-ambiguity maps predict where all models plateau.
problem: Rater disagreement is treated as perceptual noise, conflating cannot-see disagreement with cannot-agree-on-definition disagreement.
core_hypothesis: For structures with fuzzy anatomical definitions (organ boundaries at hila, vessel entry zones, gland tails), disagreement persists at high image quality, and these definitional zones form a fixed spatial map where every model's error saturates.
falsifiable_prediction: Rater disagreement in definitional zones will be nearly independent of image SNR and contrast, unlike perceptual zones; error maps of diverse architectures will share the same definitional hotspots.
why_important: It separates problems solvable by better models from problems solvable only by better ontology, redirecting research and benchmark design.
why_possibly_novel: Decomposing inter-rater variance into perceptual versus definitional components with an image-quality intervention is an uncommon experimental design in segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Have raters annotate the same anatomy at two image quality levels (native and degraded); regions where disagreement does not decrease with quality are definitional; test whether model errors of several architectures concentrate there.
main_risk: Image quality manipulation may alter rater behavior beyond perception, contaminating the decomposition.
community_default_belief: Better image quality and better models jointly reduce boundary disagreement everywhere.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Where the definition itself is contested, no amount of signal or capacity produces agreement.
fastest_falsification: If disagreement decreases uniformly with image quality across all regions, the definitional-zone concept is unnecessary.

one_line: Annotators systematically under-include ambiguous voxels, so trained models inherit an undersegmentation bias fixable by a global bias correction rather than new architectures.
problem: Segmentation error is treated as unbiased, but annotation psychology suggests asymmetric behavior: omission of uncertain voxels is cheaper for a rater than commission.
core_hypothesis: Reference masks are biased small relative to consensus-of-many, models replicate this bias, and a single learned isotropic boundary offset per structure removes most volumetric error for volumetry applications.
falsifiable_prediction: Against dense multi-rater consensus, both single-rater labels and model outputs will show statistically significant negative volume bias, and a per-structure morphological correction estimated on few cases will remove most of the volumetric error on held-out cases.
why_important: Volumetry drives therapy decisions; a two-line bias correction outperforming years of architecture work would reset priorities.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic direction of annotation bias, as opposed to its magnitude, is rarely measured or exploited as a correction target.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-rater dataset, compute signed volume error of single raters and of a standard model against high-rater-count consensus; fit and test a per-structure offset correction.
main_risk: Bias direction may differ by structure and modality, making corrections non-universal.
community_default_belief: Segmentation errors are approximately symmetric around the true boundary and must be reduced by better models.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Rater incentives are asymmetric, and consensus-of-many reveals a consistent inclusion deficit that supervised models faithfully copy.
fastest_falsification: If signed volume errors of raters and models are centered on zero against dense consensus, there is no exploitable bias.

one_line: Quality-control passes smooth reference contours, deleting real high-frequency anatomy, so models are penalized for correctly predicting fine detail.
problem: Dataset QC is assumed to only remove errors, but QC reviewers often regularize contours toward smooth, canonical shapes.
core_hypothesis: Post-QC masks have systematically lower surface frequency content than pre-QC raw annotations, and evaluation against post-QC masks ranks detail-preserving models below over-smoothing models.
falsifiable_prediction: Where pre- and post-QC annotation versions exist, spectral analysis will show high-frequency attenuation after QC, and model rankings by boundary metrics will differ between the two reference versions, favoring smoother models post-QC.
why_important: If QC injects a smoothness prior into ground truth, benchmarks structurally discourage models that recover clinically relevant fine structure such as spiculations.
why_possibly_novel: QC is audited for error removal, virtually never for the statistical fingerprint it imposes on the label distribution.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain or recreate a small annotation set with archived pre-QC versions; compare surface spectra and re-rank two models (one detail-preserving, one smooth) under each reference.
main_risk: Pre-QC annotations are rarely archived, and recreating QC realistically is hard.
community_default_belief: QC strictly improves label quality, so evaluating against QC-ed labels is strictly fairer.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Reviewers use smoothness as a proxy for correctness, which is invalid exactly for irregular pathology and detailed anatomy.
fastest_falsification: If QC leaves surface frequency statistics unchanged, the smoothing-injection claim fails immediately.

one_line: Networks fit boundary label noise late in training and interior evidence early, so per-structure early stopping at different epochs beats a single global stopping point.
problem: Memorization dynamics are well studied for classification label noise, but the spatial version for segmentation, where noise lives at boundaries, is unclear.
